top.title: City takes up a state deal to rebuild KK Avenue from Fulton Street to Lapham Boulevard
top.dek: Two new council files start design on a state-led KK reconstruction; the Fulton-to-Becher stretch is pegged at $23.1M.
top.body:
Two resolutions introduced at City Hall on Nov. 24 would line the city up with the Wisconsin Department of Transportation to rebuild S. Kinnickinnic Avenue, the state highway (WIS 32) that runs through the middle of Bay View. One covers about 1.35 miles from Fulton Street north to E. Becher Street; the other picks up at Becher and continues to Lapham Boulevard. Both were sent to the Common Council's Public Works Committee.

The state-city agreement for the Fulton-to-Becher section, dated Oct. 29, estimates the whole project at $23.1 million. Federal and state money would cover about $21 million and the city about $2.05 million. Construction is pegged at $19.55 million, including $13.5 million for the roadway itself, with $2.8 million for design and $500,000 for buying land. The Becher-to-Lapham file sets up $1.85 million for design and $200,000 for land; it doesn't list a construction estimate.

The agreement doesn't yet say what the rebuilt street would look like: the nature of the work is to be "determined by project scoping." Because the state treats parking lanes as a local cost, the city would pay the 13% of the paving bill tied to parking, plus items such as adjusting water and sewer covers.

No construction date is listed in either file. The Public Works Committee hasn't scheduled them yet; Bay View's alderperson is Marina Dimitrijevic (District 14).

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Artery Ink
spotlight.dek: Hand-drawn hearts, lungs and spines on T-shirts, made in a Bay View studio for nurses and everyone else.
spotlight.body:
Artery Ink makes clothing and gifts covered in detailed, anatomically accurate drawings of the human body: hearts, lungs, brains, spines, the digestive tract. The company works out of a studio at 2625 S. Greeley St. in Bay View, on the west side of the neighborhood near Russell Avenue, and sells mostly online, with local pickup at the studio.

It was started in 2014 by Mara Natkin, a trained illustrator, and Gloria Ramirez, a graphic designer, who met while waitressing and are now married. After losing relatives within a short span in 2013, the couple told WUWM, they took a hard look at their own health, got fascinated by how the body works and decided to put that into their art. They began with greeting cards and prints, sold at markets and shows, then quit their restaurant jobs to do it full time.

Every design is drawn by hand: Natkin lays out the piece, and Ramirez fills in the fine interior detail with a pen. Some of the more involved drawings take more than 80 hours, according to the shop's website. To get the anatomy right, they worked with a doctor and visited a cadaver lab. Health care workers became their biggest fans, and the catalog now runs from nurse, ICU and radiology shirts to awareness gear, city-themed "City Hearts" designs, stickers, pins and custom team orders.

Giving back is built in. In spring 2020 they released a "Heart of Healthcare" shirt as a fundraiser, sold about 900 in the first week and donated $12,000 to a campaign feeding frontline workers. Since then their Community Collection has put out new designs each month with proceeds going to causes, mostly Wisconsin groups. The business grew from a spare bedroom to a team of seven in a 4,800-square-foot studio, and Milwaukee Magazine featured the founders in 2018 and in a 2023 Women of Distinction section.

This week: in-stock items are 15% off through Dec. 1, with no code needed, and the shop has brought back its Rare Disease Awareness zebra-ribbon design, on pre-order through Dec. 14 to support a cause. New snowman tees and restocked holiday designs went up on the site last weekend.

Artery Ink, 2625 S. Greeley St., Suite 135. Online at arteryink.com (local pickup available; the studio isn't open weekends) and on Instagram at @arteryink.

streets.title: The rebuilt I-43 interchange at Becher Street is open, along with 4th and 5th streets
streets.dek: WisDOT reopened the Becher Street ramps Wednesday in a new diamond layout, ending a closure that began in spring.
streets.body:
The I-43/94 interchange at Becher Street, one of the main freeway connections on Bay View's west edge, reopened to traffic Wednesday, the state Department of Transportation said. S. 4th and 5th streets, the frontage streets alongside the freeway, reopened too.

The whole interchange, including Becher Street under the freeway, had been closed for reconstruction since spring, with detours sending drivers to Lapham Boulevard, 1st Street and 6th Street. The old scissor-style ramps are gone, replaced by a standard diamond interchange with rebuilt traffic signals at both ramp ends, one through lane each way on Becher under the freeway, and updated curb ramps.

WisDOT's project page has the new ramp layout and a project contact for questions.

image.alt: WisDOT notice on the Becher Street interchange reopening, with a map of the new ramps at I-43 between 4th and 5th streets

streets.title: No garbage or recycling pickup today or Friday; parking meters are off for Thanksgiving
streets.dek: Pickup days shift later after the holiday; drop-off centers reopen Saturday.
streets.body:
The city won't collect garbage or recycling today or Friday for the Thanksgiving holiday, the Department of Public Works said, and collection days shift forward after each city holiday, so plan on pickup coming later than usual this week.

Parking meters and hourly limits aren't enforced today, though cars still have to be legally parked. There's no overnight parking enforcement tonight into Friday morning, either. The city tow lot is closed today and open Friday and Saturday, and the self-help drop-off centers are closed today and Friday and reopen Saturday.

Most city offices are closed today and Friday and reopen Monday, Nov. 30. Winter overnight parking rules start Tuesday, Dec. 1.

history.title: Club Garibaldi opens: an Italian mutual aid society's corner club, 1943
history.text: In 1943 Bay View's Garibaldi Lodge turned an old corner tavern at Russell and Superior into Club Garibaldi, with orchestra dancing every Friday and Saturday.
history.body:
The corner tavern at 2501 S. Superior St. started out in 1907 as a Schlitz-built saloon serving workers from the Bay View rolling mill a block away. It passed through several owners and operators over the next three decades. Then, in January 1943, it became something new: the clubhouse of the Italian American Mutual Aid Society, whose Milwaukee chapter is named for the Italian patriot Giuseppe Garibaldi.

The society had been founded in 1908 by about 40 Italian immigrants, many of whom settled in Bay View and worked in its factories. Like other ethnic mutual aid groups of the era, it offered members help in hard times and gave the community a place to gather.

By that summer the club was advertising itself to the whole city. A Milwaukee Sentinel ad on July 10, 1943, invited readers to "come out tonite" to the new Club Garibaldi, "owned & operated by the Garibaldi Lodge," with orchestra dancing every Friday and Saturday on a "beautiful dance floor." In April 1944 the club held a grand opening for a remodeled space.

More than 80 years later, the mutual aid society still owns the building. The front room is still a neighborhood corner bar, and the old dance hall in back hosts touring bands, benefits and the Wisconsin Blues Hall of Fame's events.

weekend.intro: It's a shop-small kind of weekend in Bay View: Black Friday sales on KK, a long list of Small Business Saturday specials, and holiday pop-ups kicking off. Save room for music on Friday night and a free community dinner on Sunday.

picks.title: Small Business Saturday at URSA
picks.why: URSA anchors the KK shop-small day with 10% off and goodie-filled totes, stocked by 30-plus local businesses, for its first 50 big spenders.

picks.title: Hexed lantern craft at Chippy's
picks.why: A kid-friendly craft hour that pairs neatly with a holiday movie at the Avalon a few doors away.

picks.title: Elf pop-up returns at Lost Whale
picks.why: The bar's Elf-themed holiday makeover is back, a sure sign the season has started.

picks.title: Black Friday Yacht Rock with Reno Soul + Golden Yacht Society
picks.why: Smooth, singalong yacht rock is a good way to shake off a day of leftovers.

picks.title: Free Thanksgiving meal at Bay View United Methodist
picks.why: A free sit-down Thanksgiving dinner for anyone who wants one, no questions asked.
